question: A caller is very friendly but keeps pushing you to decide right now. You feel uncomfortable saying no. What should you do?
options: Stay on the line so you don't seem rude
Say "No, thank you" and hang up. You don't owe them a reason
Agree, then cancel later
Ask them to call back in five minutes
explanation: Being polite to a scammer only helps the scammer. Rushing you is a warning sign. You always have permission to hang up.

question: Which is a good habit for unknown phone numbers?
options: Always answer in case it's important
Let them go to voicemail. Real callers leave a message
Call back every missed number right away
Answer and stay silent
explanation: Letting unknown calls go to voicemail gives you time to think and check. Real callers leave a message you can verify.

question: An email from "Your Bank" says there's a problem with your account and has a big "Fix It Now" button. The email uses your real name. What's the safest choice?
options: Sign in through your bank's app or a web address you type yourself
Click the button, since it used your real name
Reply and ask what the problem is
Forward it to your bank's email
explanation: Scammers can find your name easily. Whatever the email looks like, go to your bank yourself instead of using its links.

question: An email says "Your Geek Squad subscription renewed for $399. Call to cancel." You never had Geek Squad. What should you do?
options: Call to cancel the charge
Ignore and delete it. Check your bank or card statement if you're unsure
Reply asking for a refund
Click the link to cancel
explanation: Fake renewal emails want you to call, where the "agent" will try to get into your computer or bank. Check your real statement instead.

question: A text says you owe $3.95 for an unpaid toll and includes a link. You did drive on a toll road recently. What should you do?
options: Pay it, since it's a small amount
Reply to ask which road
Check your toll account using the official website or app you already use
Forward it to friends to warn them
explanation: Fake toll texts are very common, and the small amount is meant to make you pay without thinking. The real goal is your card number. Check your account through the official site.

question: What's the best response to a text from an unknown number that just says "Hi, how are you?"
options: Reply politely
Ask who it is
Reply STOP
Don't reply. Delete it and block the number
explanation: Friendly texts from strangers are often the start of romance or investment scams. Not replying is the safest choice.

question: Your "granddaughter" calls crying about an emergency. You ask for the family code word and she says she forgot it. What should you do?
options: Hang up and call her, or her parents, on numbers you know
Send the money anyway, since she's upset
Ask her to call back tomorrow
Send half the money
explanation: If the caller can't give the code word, treat it as a scam. A quick call to a number you know will tell you the truth.

question: A caller from your "bank" asks you to read them the code they just texted you, to stop a fraudulent charge. What should you do?
options: Read it quickly to stop the fraud
Never share it. Hang up and call the number on your card
Read only part of it
Ask them to read it to you first
explanation: That code lets the scammer into your account. Real banks never ask for it.

question: Your screen freezes with a message: "Apple Security Alert — Your iPhone is infected. Call Apple Support at 1-888-555-0123." What's true?
options: Apple uses alerts like this
You should call quickly before your data is stolen
It's a fake web page. Close it and don't call
Only call if the number is toll-free
explanation: Apple and Microsoft never put phone numbers in warnings. Close the browser tab or app.

question: Which of these is a REAL software update?
options: A browser pop-up saying "Your Chrome is out of date, download the fix here"
An email with an update attachment
A pop-up with a phone number to call for the update
An update offered in your computer's own Settings (Windows Update, or System Settings on a Mac)
explanation: Real updates come from your device's own settings or app store, never from pop-ups, emails, or phone calls.

question: Which of these would the real IRS do?
options: Send a letter by mail explaining what you owe and your right to appeal
Call and threaten arrest unless you pay today
Ask for payment in gift cards
Text you a link to pay
explanation: Real IRS contact usually begins with a letter. It gives you time, payment options through irs.gov, and your right to disagree.

question: A text says you're eligible for a Social Security increase if you confirm your identity at "ssa-benefits-update.com." What's true?
options: You must click to get the increase
Increases happen automatically, and the real site ends in ssa.gov, so it's a scam
It's real because it mentions Social Security
Click, but only enter your name
explanation: Benefit increases are automatic. Any website not ending in .gov that claims to be Social Security is fake.

question: You're selling a chair for $100. A buyer mails a check for $1,100 and asks you to send back $1,000. What should you do?
options: Deposit the check and send the $1,000 back
Wait one day, then send the money
Don't accept it. This is an overpayment scam, and the check will bounce
Send back $900 instead
explanation: Fake checks can seem to clear, then bounce days later, and you'd owe the bank the full amount. Never accept overpayments.

question: What's the safest way to buy a used item from a stranger online?
options: Pay a deposit by Zelle first
Have it shipped after paying with a gift card
Wire money to the seller
Meet in a public place, see the item, then pay
explanation: Seeing the item in person before paying protects you. Many police stations have safe exchange spots.

question: Your online sweetheart, whom you've never met, asks you to help with their plane ticket so they can finally visit. What should you do?
options: Don't send money. Talk to a trusted friend or family member
Pay, since they're finally coming
Send gift cards instead
Pay half and they pay half
explanation: The visit that needs your money is a classic romance scam ending. Talking it over with someone you trust can break the spell.

question: Which is a HEALTHY sign in a new online relationship?
options: They say "I love you" in the first week
They suggest a video call and meeting in a public place
They need money for an emergency
They ask you to keep the relationship secret
explanation: Real people are happy to video chat and meet in public. Rushing, secrecy, and money requests are warning signs.

question: A new online friend shows you how they made $10,000 on a crypto app and offers to help you start. What should you do?
options: Start with a small amount
Ask for screenshots first
Decline. Online friends who push investing are a common scam
Invest only what you can afford to lose
explanation: Fake friendships that lead to investing are one of the most costly scams today. The app and the profits are fake.

question: You realize you've been scammed out of money. What should you do?
options: Keep it to yourself because you're embarrassed
Pay a recovery company to get it back
Send more money to unlock the account
Call your bank or payment company right away, and report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov
explanation: Acting fast gives you the best chance of stopping more losses. Reporting is free and helps protect others. Scams happen to smart people, and there's no shame in it.
